title: Anthropic adds new Claude rule banning recreations of existing games
content:
Anthropic has changed its Claude Code tool so that it won’t recreate specific existing video games, following growing concern from developers about their games being cloned.
The change was spotted around October 27 by X user Chasm before Anthropic said anything publicly. The new rule tells Claude: “Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.”
Anthropic has since confirmed the change, with Addy Osmani, a member of technical staff, explaining in a post on X that the rule was added because using Claude to infringe on IP breaks the company’s usage policy.
“We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy,” he wrote.
“Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.”
Developers have been worried about clones
The change comes as more developers worry about their work being copied before it even launches. Alliance Arts recently cancelled the public demo for its upcoming Steam game Drunken Goddess Reflux, warning that its content “could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game’s presentation and gameplay with AI.”
Other developers have been pressing Valve on how it plans to stop clones from flooding Steam.
How well the new rule works remains to be seen, as Claude has no way of checking whether a user actually owns the game they’re working on, and other models that can be run locally don’t have the same restrictions.
Osmani said Anthropic will “continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance,” and asked anyone who has their own project turned down by mistake to contact him.

report.summary: Anthropic added a Claude Code rule barring recreation of specific existing games, citing IP policy, as developers worry about AI clones.
report.background: The change lands amid a broader collision between fast generative AI and game development. AI coding agents can now produce playable prototypes from a short prompt, collapsing work that once took teams months. That has alarmed indie developers, who fear a distinctive mechanic or visual style can be cloned before launch, and storefronts like Steam face pressure to police lookalikes. Anthropic’s rule is a prompt-level guardrail, not a copyright detection system: it tells the model to avoid recreating a specific existing game, even if renamed. The update was spotted around October 27 before Anthropic confirmed it publicly, highlighting how model behavior can shift quietly through system prompts. It also reflects a wider industry debate over whether AI vendors should block potential infringement at generation time or leave responsibility to users and platforms.
key_points: Anthropic added a line to Claude Code’s instructions telling it not to “build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.” The change was spotted around October 27 by a user before Anthropic publicly acknowledged it, showing how system-prompt tweaks can alter developer tool behavior without a formal product launch.

Anthropic staffer Addy Osmani said the rule exists because using Claude to infringe intellectual property violates its usage policy. He stressed that “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working,” framing the restriction as narrow rather than a ban on game development assistance.

The move follows developer alarm over AI cloning. Alliance Arts cancelled the public demo of Drunken Goddess Reflux, warning its content could be used to imitate its presentation and gameplay with AI, while other developers have pressed Valve on stopping clones from flooding Steam. The rule responds to those fears but does not resolve them.

Enforcement is limited. Claude cannot verify whether a user owns or has rights to the game they ask it to recreate, and locally run models lack the same restrictions. Osmani said Anthropic will keep iterating and asked developers wrongly refused to report cases, suggesting false positives and workarounds are expected.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the rule signals a shift toward prompt-level IP guardrails in coding agents, even without reliable detection. It may push model providers to document policy changes and compete on copyright safety, while open and local models remain harder to govern. For developers, the practical effect is more caution: teams may need to document asset provenance, avoid “make it like X” prompts, and design original mechanics. It also gives studios a talking point when asking platforms to act. For regular users, one-prompt game clones may become less reliable, and some legitimate requests could be refused, but the change does not stop cloning via other models, modified prompts, or manual recreation.
report.tools: Watch Claude Code’s policy prompts and release notes, plus Cursor and Windsurf for similar IP guardrails. For original game building, try open-source engines Godot, Bevy, and LÖVE; for local-model experimentation, Ollama or LM Studio show how restrictions differ. Developers concerned about provenance can track asset licenses and use GitHub’s Copilot content-exclusion features where relevant.
